quote.text: Between 2012 and 2025, 208 papers in all fields named both Akron and Case Western, eight of them classified in polymers, and the two hold three joint NSF projects, the newest starting in 2017 (OpenAlex and NSF).

plant.text: Check Akron and Case Western separately for polymer work: of 208 papers naming both, eight are classified in polymers, and no new joint NSF award started after 2017, through 2025.

claims.text: The University of Akron and Case Western Reserve are both named on more than 200 works since 2012 (one author holding both affiliations is enough to count a work) and hold three joint NSF projects (six award IDs, since NSF splits a Collaborative Research project into one award per institution).
claims.source: OpenAlex works listing both institutions; NSF awards API only; all fields
claims.assert: 200 < D['totals']['coauthored'] < 300 and D['totals']['joint_awards'] == 3 and sum(len(a['id'].split(' + ')) for a in D['joint_awards']) == 6 and sorted(a['id'] for a in D['joint_awards']) == ['1432891 + 1432950', '1711625 + 1711395', '1731722 + 1730946'] and all(a['via'] == 'separate awards, one project' and len(set(a['id'].split(' + '))) == len(a['id'].split(' + ')) == 2 for a in D['joint_awards'])
claims.falsified_if: Either measure stops matching the words beside it: the coauthored count falling to 200 or below makes 'more than 200' false, reaching 300 makes it the wrong floor to print, and the award count leaving three contradicts a heading that spells the number out. The old assertion was `> 150` against a text reading 'more than 200' and `>= 3` against a text and a heading both reading 'four', so a count of 151 and three awards would have passed while the page said otherwise. This is the claim that refutes the deleted 'nothing suggests they have met' line; if it fails, that line was closer to right than this page is and the page must be withdrawn, not softened. It is about collaboration EXISTING, and is deliberately independent of whether the collaboration is about polymers — see col-rarely-about-polymers, which says it mostly is not. [Round 6, 2026-09-28: the page said the universities 'have written 208 papers together' and 'coauthored' them, and that a counted paper is evidence 'two people worked together'. The count filters on affiliations only, so one author listing both universities satisfies it; a live OpenAlex query that day found 15 of 211 such works with both universities carried by a single author. The page now says 208 papers NAME both. The assert also requires every joint project to carry exactly two distinct award IDs, because eight IDs in total do not stop one project from holding one and another three. Which institution holds which ID is not in the shipped data and is not checked.] [Round 7, 2026-09-28: nor which project an award ID belongs to. joint_awards stores one title per pair of IDs, so exchanging IDs between two projects keeps two distinct IDs on each and eight in all (Codex); only the NSF records can settle it.] [Round 9, 2026-09-29: the page said four projects and eight award IDs. One pair, 1620198 (Case Western, 2016) and 1852597 (Akron, 2018), shares one sole PI, Lingxing Yao (NSF piId 269970204): a researcher moving between the universities, not a joint project; its partner was the University of Minnesota (1620316). fetch_collab.py now drops a title pair whose awards share a PI. The shipped data carries no PI, so the assert pins the exact set of award-ID pairs the NSF records were checked against that day; reinstating the transfer, or any refetch that adds or changes a pair, fails it until the new pair's PIs are read.]

claims.text: Papers naming both peaked at 29 in 2018, dropped to 11, came back to 22 in 2020, then fell in four straight years to two papers in 2024 and rose to six in 2025; the controlled rate is still 63 percent below the peak. This guards the standfirst's shape sentence, the hero chart's description, the cold open's label and the closer. THE SHAPE MOVED TWICE ON 2026-08-31. The page had been fetched on 2026-08-17 with the window hand-stopped at 2024 and said joint output 'has fallen in each of the last three' years. First, the same keyless OpenAlex call now returns 2025, and 2025 tripled off the 2024 floor. Second, deriving the run instead of counting it showed the run was never three: 2021 already fell from 2020, so the falls into the trough are FOUR, and the sentence before it that put 2021 in a three-year wobble was describing a shape the chart did not draw. The fall is still real and the rebound is one year on six papers, so the page reports both and headlines neither: app.js walks the run back from the lowest year rather than carrying a hand-set three.
claims.source: as above; works naming both per 1,000 of Akron's own annual output
claims.assert: [r['year'] for r in D['series']] == list(range(2012, 2026)) and D['totals']['peak_year'] == 2018 and D['totals']['peak_joint'] == 29 and max(r['joint'] for r in D['series']) == 29 and D['series'][-1]['year'] == 2025 and (lambda s: s[2019] < s[2018] and s[2019] == 11 and s[2020] > s[2019] and s[2020] == 22 and s[2021] < s[2020] and s[2022] < s[2021] and s[2023] < s[2022] and s[2024] < s[2023] and s[2024] == 2 and min(sorted(s), key=s.get) == 2024 and s[2025] == 6)({r['year']: r['joint'] for r in D['series']}) and (lambda q: q[2021] < q[2020] and q[2022] < q[2021] and q[2023] < q[2022] and q[2024] < q[2023] and q[2025] > q[2024])({r['year']: r['per_1k_akron'] for r in D['series']}) and (lambda pk: pk['joint'] == 29 and sum(r['per_1k_akron'] == pk['per_1k_akron'] for r in D['series']) == 1 and pk['per_1k_akron'] == max(r['per_1k_akron'] for r in D['series']) and tofixed((1 - D['series'][-1]['per_1k_akron'] / pk['per_1k_akron']) * 100, 0) == '63')(one(r for r in D['series'] if r['year'] == D['totals']['peak_year']))
claims.actual: (lambda a: a + [tofixed((1 - D['series'][-1]['per_1k_akron'] / one(r for r in D['series'] if r['year'] == D['totals']['peak_year'])['per_1k_akron']) * 100, 0)])([(r['year'], r['joint'], r['akron'], r['per_1k_akron']) for r in D['series']])
claims.falsified_if: The peak moves off 2018 or off 29 works, 2019 stops being the drop or 2020 the rebound, the run of four falls into 2024 breaks or lengthens, 2024 stops being the lowest year at two papers (or the earliest of tied lowest years, which is the one app.js walks back from), 2025 stops printing six, the controlled rate stops falling across the same four years or stops rebounding after them, or the end-of-series gap to the peak stops rounding to 63 percent. Any of those and the standfirst, the cold-open label and the closer are describing a shape the chart beneath them does not draw. The 2020 boundary is asserted in both directions because it is what makes the run FOUR rather than three or five, and a hand-set three is the error this claim was rewritten to catch. The falls are asserted on the COUNTS and again on the CONTROLLED RATE, because the closer walks the reader down the rate and the two series could diverge. NOTE the final year is the least-indexed and must not carry this claim alone: the 2018-2024 movement holds without it.

claims.text: Case Western's indexed output at the end of the series is at least as high as at the joint peak. That comparison cannot rule out delays in indexing papers naming both.
claims.source: OpenAlex, each institution's own works per year
claims.assert: D['series'][-1]['cwru'] >= [r['cwru'] for r in D['series'] if r['year'] == D['totals']['peak_year']][0]
claims.actual: [(r['year'], r['akron'], r['cwru']) for r in D['series'][-4:]]
claims.falsified_if: Case Western's indexed output drops below its level in the joint peak year. This checks the stated comparison only; neither outcome identifies indexing delay or its absence.

claims.text: Within the window measured here, 2012 to 2025, no new joint NSF award started after 2017.
claims.source: NSF awards API, awards to either institution since 2012, Collaborative Research mechanism only; all fields
claims.assert: max(int((a['start'] or '0000')[-4:]) for a in D['joint_awards']) <= 2017 and D['meta']['years'][1] == 2025
claims.actual: [(a['start'], a['amount'], a['title'][:60]) for a in D['joint_awards']] + [('window', D['meta']['years'])]
claims.falsified_if: A joint award starting after 2017 and inside the window appears, OR the pull is extended past 2025 without re-reading this sentence. The window end is asserted as an EQUALITY for exactly that reason, and it did its job on 2026-08-31: the pull moved from 2024 to 2025 and this claim failed until every sentence carrying a window year had been re-read. LIMIT, and it has already bitten: the unbounded form of this claim ('none since 2017') was refutable from PIC's own timeline page, which records the CWRU-led NEO-SMART NSF Engine awarded 2026-07-13. That award is outside this window, so the arithmetic held while the sentence did not. Separately, this sees NSF only: a joint NIH, DOE, EDA or state award would not appear here and would not falsify the arithmetic while still making the sentence misleading. [Round 8, 2026-09-28: the page's closing paragraph still carried the unbounded form beside the standfirst that names NEO-SMART; it now states the window (Codex). Claims read data, not the page, so no assert can hold that sentence.]

claims.text: In those years 208 papers named both universities, of which eight are classified in polymers, and the two hold three joint NSF projects worth $3.4 million, the newest of the projects starting in 2017.
claims.source: NSF awards API, Collaborative Research projects with one award at each institution; OpenAlex works listing both institutions
claims.assert: D['totals']['coauthored'] == 208 and D['totals']['polymer_total'] == 8 and D['totals']['joint_awards'] == len(D['joint_awards']) == 3 and D['totals']['joint_award_dollars'] == sum(a['amount'] for a in D['joint_awards']) and tofixed(D['totals']['joint_award_dollars'] / 1e6, 1) == '3.4' and max(int(a['start'][-4:]) for a in D['joint_awards']) == 2017 and D['totals']['newest_joint_award_year'] == '2017'
claims.actual: (lambda a: a + (tofixed(a[3] / 1e6, 1),))((D['totals']['coauthored'], D['totals']['polymer_total'], len(D['joint_awards']), sum(a['amount'] for a in D['joint_awards']), sorted(int(a['start'][-4:]) for a in D['joint_awards'])))
claims.falsified_if: The paper or polymer count moves, the project count moves off three, the three amounts stop summing to the stored total or that total stops rounding to $3.4 million, or the newest start year is anything but 2017. The standfirst's bold sentence was typed by hand while the hero figures below it read the same dollars and year from the data (added 2026-09-29), so a refetch could have moved the figures and left the standfirst. 'Newest starting in 2017' is checked as the latest start year equal to 2017, not merely no later than it, which is all col-no-new-joint-award asks. [2026-09-30: the assertion reads the data, so a standfirst retyped with a wrong dollar figure or year would still have passed it. `counts` now binds the printed sentence, read by verify_nouns.py from the page as rendered: "projects worth $3.4 million" must follow "three joint NSF", and "projects starting in 2017" must follow "the newest of the". Any other dollar figure or year in either place fails as a figure not on the page.]

counts.noun: name both Akron and Case Western

claims.text: These instruments can demonstrate collaboration and cannot demonstrate its absence.
claims.source: Method note, not a data check
claims.falsified_if: Nothing in the data can falsify this; it is the standing limit on how the page may be read, and it is the reason a null result would not have been published.

claims.text: Of 208 papers naming both, eight are classified in polymers and plastics and eleven in biomaterials. A paper can carry both, so at most nineteen are in either subject and at least 90 percent in neither. The four years 2021 to 2024 carry no paper naming both in either subject; 2025 carries one, the first since 2020.
claims.source: OpenAlex subfields 2507 and 2502, confirmed against the s3://openalex snapshot; a classification, not a keyword
claims.assert: D['totals']['subject_total'] == D['totals']['polymer_total'] + D['totals']['bio_total'] == sum(r['polymer'] + r['bio'] for r in D['series']) and int(100 * (1 - D['totals']['subject_total'] / D['totals']['coauthored'])) == 90 and D['totals']['polymer_total'] == 8 and D['totals']['bio_total'] == 11 and D['totals']['last_subject_year'] == 2025 and all(r['polymer'] + r['bio'] == 0 for r in D['series'] if 2021 <= r['year'] <= 2024) and one(r['polymer'] for r in D['series'] if r['year'] == 2025) == 1 and one(r['bio'] for r in D['series'] if r['year'] == 2025) == 0 and sorted(r['year'] for r in D['series'] if r['polymer'] + r['bio'])[-2] == 2020
claims.actual: [(r['year'], r['polymer'], r['bio']) for r in D['series']] + [(D['totals']['coauthored'], D['totals']['subject_total'], D['totals']['last_subject_year'])]
claims.falsified_if: The subject share rises above 15 percent, either subject count moves off eight and eleven, or the four-year silence from 2021 to 2024 gains a paper. THE SENTENCE THIS GUARDS WAS INVERTED BY A REFRESH: it read 'the last of either was 2020', which was a four-year silence written as a date, and the 2026-08-31 pull put one polymer paper in 2025 and made it read as recency. It now measures the silence, which is what it was always about. THIS NUMBER ALSO MOVED WHEN THE BOUND DID: the full-text keyword 'polymer' returned 24 of these papers and the subject classification returns eight, because the keyword counted any paper that mentioned the word. The larger number was the one published first. [Round 8, 2026-09-28: subject_total is the sum of the two subject counts, not their union. A live OpenAlex query found two works naming both universities in both subfields (W2553059811, 2016; W2597373224, 2017), and the cache stores no intersection, so the page prints nineteen as a ceiling and the share in neither subject as a floor (Codex). A refetch should pull the union of work IDs.]
claims.breaks_if: A fresh pull changes the 208 papers naming both, or the eight in polymers.
claims.guards: 208 papers since 2012 name both Akron and Case Western. Eight are classified in polymers.
